commitResults.messageTitle: Level-0: Rename Duke to MattChatBot, greet and exit
commitResults.messageBody:
Rename the chatbot to MattChatBot and remove all traces of the placeholder
Duke name from the code and the docs, so the product has an identity of its
own rather than the template's.

Replace the banner-only main method with separate greet() and exit() steps.
Splitting them now leaves a clear seam where the command loop goes in
Level-1, instead of having to break apart a single long main later. The
banner uses a text block rather than concatenated "\n" strings, which keeps
the ASCII art readable and editable in the source.

Fill in the student profile in AGENTS.md and add command-line build/run
instructions to the README, since the project is being developed in VS Code
rather than IntelliJ.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-1: Echo user commands until bye
commitResults.messageBody:
Add an input loop between the greeting and the farewell, echoing each line
back to the user and stopping on the bye command.

Guard the loop with hasNextLine() rather than calling nextLine() in an
infinite loop, so that input ending without an explicit bye (Ctrl-D at the
keyboard, or piped input running out) exits cleanly instead of throwing
NoSuchElementException.

Extract a say() helper, since the greeting, the echo and the farewell all
wrap their output in the same dividers; this also gives later increments one
place to change the reply format.

Update the README sample output, which still showed the bot exiting
immediately rather than waiting for commands.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-2: Store and list user input
commitResults.messageBody:
Replace the echo behaviour with simple command handling: the list command
prints everything stored so far, numbered from 1, and any other input is
stored and confirmed with "added: <text>".

Store items in a fixed String[100] with a separate count, as the requirements
allow and cap at 100 items. Guard the add path so that exceeding the cap
reports that the list is full rather than throwing
ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, and report an empty list explicitly rather
than printing a blank block. Blank input lines are ignored so they do not
become empty entries.

Rename echoUntilBye() to runCommandLoop(), as it no longer echoes, and update
the README sample output to show the new add/list behaviour.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-3: Mark tasks as done, add Task class
commitResults.messageBody:
Add mark and unmark commands so the user can set and reverse a task's done
status, and show that status in the list output, which now carries the
"Here are the tasks in your list:" header and a [X] or [ ] box per task.

Follow the A-Classes extension required by this increment: introduce a Task
class in its own file, holding the description together with its done state.
A plain String had nowhere to keep that state, so the stored items had to
become objects; Task also owns its own display format via toString(), which
keeps the rendering next to the data it describes.

Split input on the first space so that mark and unmark can be told apart from
task descriptions that merely start with those words. Reject a missing,
non-numeric or out-of-range task number with a message instead of throwing;
proper error handling arrives in Level-5.

Update the README sample output, and its compile command, which now needs to
cover both source files.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-4: Add todos, deadlines and events
commitResults.messageBody:
Add todo, deadline and event commands so the bot tracks the three task types
required by this increment. Deadlines take a /by and events take a /from and
a /to; dates stay as free text, as the requirements allow at this stage.

Follow the A-Inheritance extension required by this increment: Todo, Deadline
and Event now extend Task, rather than Task carrying a type field and a
branch for each type. Task becomes abstract with an abstract getTypeIcon(),
since nothing creates a typeless task any more and each subclass can supply
its own marker; Deadline and Event extend toString() via super, so the
"[T][X] description" prefix is defined in exactly one place.

Unrecognised input can no longer be stored verbatim, because a bare string
has no task type, so it now reports the available commands instead.
Malformed todo, deadline and event commands report the expected form rather
than storing a half-built task; Level-5 replaces these ad hoc checks with
proper error handling.

Update the README sample output to cover the three task types.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-5: Handle invalid input with exceptions
commitResults.messageBody:
Follow the A-Exceptions extension required by this increment: add a
MattChatBotException carrying a message written for the user, throw it from
the command methods, and catch it in one place in the command loop. The loop
reports the message and continues, so a bad command never ends the session.
Making it a checked exception means the compiler requires every command path
to either handle the problem or pass it up to that single reporting point.

Handle every error the current version can hit, not only the two shown in the
requirements: unknown commands, a todo with no description, a deadline or
event missing its /by, /from or /to or the text after them, a task number
that is missing, non-numeric or outside the list, and a full list.

Locate /by, /from and /to by position rather than splitting on " /by "
surrounded by spaces. The previous approach reported "needs a /by" for
"deadline /by Sunday" and for a trailing "/by" with nothing after it, since
neither has the surrounding spaces the split looked for; both messages named
the wrong problem. Searching for /to only after /from also stops a
description that mentions /to from being read as the end time.

Update the README with an example of an error reply.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-6: Delete tasks, store them in an ArrayList
commitResults.messageBody:
Add a delete command that removes a task by its list number and reports what
was removed along with how many tasks remain.

Follow the A-Collections extension required by this increment: replace the
fixed Task[100] and its separate count with an ArrayList. The list now grows
as needed, so the 100-task ceiling and the "list is full" error are gone, and
removal closes the gap by itself rather than needing a shift loop. Task
numbers therefore renumber after a delete, which the requirements' example
relies on.

Reuse the existing task-number parsing for delete, so a missing, non-numeric
or out-of-range number is reported the same way as for mark and unmark.
Extract countSummary() and describeCount(), now that both add and delete
report the remaining count.

Update the README to cover the delete command.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-Enums: Represent commands as an enum
commitResults.messageBody:
Replace the string literals driving command dispatch with a Command enum,
each constant holding the keyword the user types.

The keywords previously existed in two places: as literals in the dispatch
switch, and again inside the "I don't know what that means" message listing
them. Nothing kept the two in step, and adding delete in Level-6 required
remembering to update both. The message is now generated from the enum, so
the list cannot go stale.

Dispatch is now a switch expression over the enum rather than a switch
statement over strings. Since every branch yields the exit flag, the compiler
requires the switch to be exhaustive: adding a constant to Command fails the
build until it is handled, which a string switch with a default branch could
never catch. Messages that named a command now read the keyword from the enum
for the same reason.

Behaviour is unchanged, including case-insensitive command words.

commitResults.messageTitle: Save tasks to disk on every change
commitResults.messageBody:
The task list only existed in memory, so everything the user entered
was lost when the chatbot exited.

Add a Storage class that writes the list to data/mattchatbot.txt, and
call it from every operation that changes the list: add, delete, mark
and unmark.

Each task type encodes itself through toFileFormat(), so the knowledge
of what a deadline or an event needs to record stays with that class
instead of collecting in a switch inside Storage.

Storage rewrites the whole file rather than appending. Appending is
cheaper, but cannot express a deletion or a change of status, so it
would not stay correct.

The save path is built from separate name parts and is relative, so it
works on any operating system and wherever the project folder is copied
to. The data folder is created if it does not exist yet, and is git
ignored, being runtime data rather than source.

commitResults.messageTitle: Load saved tasks on startup
commitResults.messageBody:
Tasks were being written to disk but never read back, so each session
still started empty and the saved file was pointless.

Read the file during startup and use its contents as the starting task
list, so a session continues where the previous one left off.

A missing file is treated as an empty list rather than an error. That is
exactly what a first run looks like on a computer that has never run the
chatbot before, so it is normal rather than a fault.

Parsing dispatches on the type marker that toFileFormat() writes, which
keeps the reading and writing formats defined next to each other.

commitResults.messageTitle: Handle a corrupted save file
commitResults.messageBody:
A damaged line in the save file crashed the chatbot on startup with an
ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, because parsing read fields that a short
line did not have. A file edited by hand, or truncated by a crash during
a save, would make the chatbot unusable.

Validate each line before reading its fields: check the type marker, the
field count expected for that type, a non-blank description, and a
status of 0 or 1.

Skip a line that fails those checks and carry on with the rest of the
file, rather than abandoning the whole list. One damaged line should not
cost the user every other task they saved.

Report the number of skipped lines at startup, so the loss is visible
rather than silent. The next change to the list rewrites the file
without the damaged lines.

commitResults.messageTitle: Document task saving in the README
commitResults.messageBody:
The README described the commands but not that tasks now outlive a
session, which is the behaviour a new user would most likely wonder
about.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-Level-7'
commitResults.messageBody:
Level-7 saves the task list to disk whenever it changes and loads it back
at startup, so tasks survive between sessions. Damaged lines in the save
file are skipped and reported rather than crashing the chatbot.

commitResults.messageTitle: Store deadline and event dates as date-times
commitResults.messageBody:
Dates were kept as free text, so the chatbot could not tell that
"2019-10-15" is a date at all, let alone compare two of them or show one
in a friendlier form.

Store them as java.time.LocalDateTime instead. Accept yyyy-MM-dd, with
an optional time as HHmm, and display them as MMM dd yyyy, so the format
read in is deliberately different from the format shown back.

Put parsing and formatting in a DateTimes class, so the accepted input
formats and the displayed format are defined next to each other rather
than spread across the task types that use them.

A task entered without a time is stored at midnight and displayed as a
bare date. This means a task genuinely due at 00:00 also shows as a bare
date, which is cheaper than carrying a separate flag on every task to
record whether a time was given.

Free text such as "Sunday" is now rejected when entered, and lines using
it in an existing save file are skipped and reported by the handling
added in Level-7, rather than crashing the chatbot.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add an on command to list tasks by date
commitResults.messageBody:
Storing real dates is only worth doing if something uses them, so add
the command the requirements suggest as a stretch goal: on <date> lists
the tasks falling on that date.

Ask each task whether it occurs on the date, rather than testing its
type with instanceof from the outside. Todos answer false by default,
and the types that carry dates override it, so a future task type
decides its own answer.

An event counts as occurring on every date it spans, not only the day it
starts, so a week-long event shows up on each day of that week.

commitResults.messageTitle: Update the README for dated tasks
commitResults.messageBody:
The README still showed deadlines written as "Sunday" and events as
"Mon 2pm", which the chatbot now rejects, so following it would have
produced errors.

Show the yyyy-MM-dd format, the optional time, and the new on command.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-Level-8'
commitResults.messageBody:
Level-8 stores deadline and event dates as java.time date-times rather
than free text, accepting yyyy-MM-dd with an optional HHmm time and
displaying them as MMM dd yyyy. It also adds an on command that lists
the tasks falling on a given date.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract Ui to handle user interaction
commitResults.messageBody:
The main class held the divider, the banner, every printed message and
the Scanner, mixed in with the logic that decided what to do. Changing
how a reply looked meant editing the class that also managed the task
list.

Move all reading and printing into a Ui class. The rest of the code now
decides what happened and asks Ui to say it, so the wording and layout
of replies live in one place.

This also isolates the assumption that the chatbot talks through the
console, which is the part that would have to change first if the
interface were ever replaced.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract TaskList to own the task list
commitResults.messageBody:
The list was a bare ArrayList held by the main class, so the rules about
it were spread across the callers. In particular, every command that
referred to a task by number had to remember to range check it before
indexing, and the parser was doing that check even though it knew
nothing about the list.

Move the list and its rules into a TaskList class. Bounds checking now
happens inside get() and remove(), so a task number that names nothing
reports the same way whichever command was used, and cannot be indexed
by a caller that forgot to check.

Move the "occurs on this date" search and the singular/plural task count
here too, since both are questions about the list rather than about the
chatbot.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract Parser to interpret user input
commitResults.messageBody:
Reading the input was spread through the main class: splitting off the
command word, hunting for the /by and /from markers, converting task
numbers and dates. Those are all statements about the input syntax, not
about what the chatbot does, and they sat next to the code that acted on
them.

Move them into a Parser class that returns things the rest of the code
can use directly: a Command, a ready-built Task, a list position, a
date. The main class now reads as a list of what each command does.

Parser converts a task number but does not check whether it exists,
since how many tasks there are is TaskList's business. Keeping that
split means neither class has to know the other's rules.

commitResults.messageTitle: Give Storage and the chatbot a proper instance
commitResults.messageBody:
Storage was a class of static methods with the save path baked into a
constant, and the chatbot itself was entirely static. Nothing could hold
two of either, and nothing could point Storage at a different file,
which a test will need.

Give Storage a constructor taking the path, and turn its methods into
instance methods. Give MattChatBot a constructor that builds its Ui,
Storage and TaskList, and a run() method holding the session, so main()
is one line that creates a chatbot and runs it.

Report a loading problem after the welcome rather than during
construction, so the greeting still comes first.

Storage now takes a TaskList rather than a raw ArrayList, so the two
classes that deal in whole task lists agree on the same type.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-MoreOOP'
commitResults.messageBody:
A-MoreOOP extracts Ui, TaskList, Parser and an instance-based Storage
from the main class, and turns MattChatBot itself into an object with a
constructor and a run() method. Behaviour is unchanged.

commitResults.messageTitle: Organize classes into packages
commitResults.messageBody:
All twelve classes sat directly in the source root, so nothing in the
layout said which classes belonged together, and the folder would only
get harder to read as more classes arrive.

Put them under seedu.mattchatbot, with the task types and the list that
holds them in seedu.mattchatbot.task. That goes beyond the minimum of a
single package, because the task classes form an obvious group that the
rest of the code uses through a small number of entry points.

src/main/java stays the source root, with the package folders inside it,
since later tools expect to find sources there.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-Packages'
commitResults.messageBody:
A-Packages moves the classes under seedu.mattchatbot, with the task
types and TaskList in seedu.mattchatbot.task.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'add-gradle-support'
Point the Gradle build at MattChatBot
commitResults.messageBody:
The build file merged from add-gradle-support names seedu.duke.Duke as
the main class and duke.jar as the JAR, neither of which exists in this
project.

Point mainClass at seedu.mattchatbot.MattChatBot and name the JAR
mattchatbot.jar, so gradlew run and gradlew shadowJar work.

Ignore the build output directory, which Gradle regenerates and which
should not be committed, and document the Gradle commands in the README.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add JUnit tests for the parsing and storage classes
commitResults.messageBody:
Nothing verified the code except running the chatbot by hand, so a
regression could only be noticed by someone remembering to try the right
command.

Add 50 tests across four classes, covering the parts most likely to hold
bugs: Parser reading each command form and rejecting each malformed one,
TaskList bounds and the date search, DateTimes formats, and Storage
round-tripping a file. Storage tests write inside a JUnit temporary
folder, so they never touch the real save file.

The tests found two real bugs, both fixed here.

Storage turned its path into name parts and rebuilt them from an empty
first element, which silently dropped the leading separator of an
absolute path and wrote to the wrong place. It now converts the path
whole, which is portable anyway because Java accepts "/" as a separator
on every platform.

Date parsing used the default resolver, which quietly moved an
impossible date such as 2019-02-30 to the last day of the month instead
of rejecting it. Parsing is now strict, which also means using the
proleptic year "uuuu" rather than "yyyy".

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-JUnit'
commitResults.messageBody:
A-JUnit adds 50 tests across Parser, TaskList, DateTimes and Storage,
and fixes the two bugs those tests uncovered: an absolute save path
losing its leading separator, and impossible dates being silently
adjusted rather than rejected.

commitResults.messageTitle: Remove stray files written by the failing tests
commitResults.messageBody:
The first run of the new Storage tests wrote into a var/folders/... tree
inside the project. That was the bug those tests had just caught: an
absolute temporary path lost its leading separator and became a relative
one, so the files landed under the project root instead of the system
temporary folder.

The bug is fixed, but the files it produced were committed alongside the
fix. Remove them; nothing refers to them.

commitResults.messageTitle: Document building the distributable JAR
commitResults.messageBody:
The shadow plugin merged in with Gradle support already produces a JAR
with its dependencies bundled, but nothing said how to build or run it.

Document gradlew shadowJar and the java -jar command the requirements
expect users to run. The JAR itself stays out of the repository, since
it is a generated binary; it is published through a GitHub release
instead.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add the missing JavaDoc header comments
commitResults.messageBody:
Most classes and methods already carried header comments, but the
javadoc tool still reported twelve warnings, which are exactly the
places a reader would find undocumented.

Document main(), every constant of the Command enum, and the Command
constructor. Add the @return tags missing from getKeyword(),
listKeywords(), size() and isEmpty().

Give Parser and DateTimes explicit private constructors, and Ui a
documented public one. Java supplies an undocumented default constructor
otherwise, and for the two utility classes a private constructor also
states that they are not meant to be instantiated.

The javadoc task now completes with no warnings, so the tool itself
checks this from here on.

commitResults.messageTitle: Rename boolean query methods to follow the standard
commitResults.messageBody:
The coding standard asks that boolean methods read as questions, using
an is, has, was, can or should prefix. Task.occursOn(date) returned a
boolean without one.

Rename it to isOn(date), so call sites read as the question they ask:
task.isOn(date). Rename TaskList.occurringOn to getTasksOn for the same
reason in reverse, since that one returns tasks rather than a boolean
and should not read like a question.

Import java.util.List in StorageTest rather than writing java.util.List
inline, since the standard asks for explicit imports over fully
qualified names.

Checked the rest of the code against the standard's mechanical rules:
no tabs, no wildcard imports, no line over the 110 character soft limit,
array brackets attached to the type, braces on every conditional body,
and no public non-constant fields.

commitResults.messageTitle: Record the coding standard in AGENTS.md
commitResults.messageBody:
The standard applies to all code added from here on, not only the code
tweaked for this increment, so state it where future work will see it
rather than leaving it implicit.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a find command to search task descriptions
commitResults.messageBody:
The list could only be shown whole or filtered by date, so picking one
task out of a long list meant reading the whole thing.

Add find <keyword>, which shows the tasks whose description contains the
keyword, ignoring case. Matching happens anywhere in the description
rather than on whole words only, so a partial word finds a task too.

Search the description alone, not the formatted dates, so that a keyword
like "Oct" does not silently match every task in October when the user
meant to search for text.

Expose the description through a getter rather than reaching into the
field, and put the search in TaskList beside the date search, since both
are questions about the list.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-JavaDoc'
commitResults.messageBody:
A-JavaDoc documents main(), the Command constants and constructor, adds
the missing @return tags, and gives the utility classes explicit
constructors, so the javadoc task reports no warnings.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-CodingStandard'
Merge branch 'branch-Level-9'
commitResults.messageBody:
Level-9 adds a find command that searches task descriptions for a
keyword, ignoring case.

Two conflicts had to be resolved, both caused by the three branches
being written without sight of each other.

Command.java conflicted textually: Level-9 inserted FIND between ON and
MARK, exactly where A-JavaDoc had added a header comment to every
constant. Both changes are wanted, so FIND is kept in its place with a
header comment of its own.

TaskList had a quieter clash that Git merged without complaint.
A-CodingStandard renamed occurringOn to getTasksOn, while Level-9 added
a search method called matching. Merged together, two neighbouring
methods that answer the same kind of question were named by different
conventions, so matching is renamed to getTasksMatching.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add Checkstyle to the build
commitResults.messageBody:
Until now the SE-EDU coding standard was only enforced by reading the code.
Checkstyle checks it mechanically, so a violation fails the build instead of
waiting to be noticed in a review.

The config in config/checkstyle is the one from AddressBook Level 3, which
encodes the same standard the project already follows, and the suppressions
file exempts test classes from the type-level Javadoc rules.

Fixing the 74 violations it reported meant four kinds of change:

- separating the project's own imports from the java.* ones with a blank
  line, and sorting java.util.ArrayList before java.util.List
- moving the private "not meant to be instantiated" constructors in Parser
  and DateTimes below the constants, and lifting Storage's SEPARATOR above
  its instance field, since static members are declared first
- lifting the "() ->" of each assertThrows lambda onto the previous line, as
  a separator may not start a line
- indenting the case labels inside the three switch expressions

None of these change behaviour; the tests and javadoc still pass.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-CheckStyle'
Add a JavaFX GUI
commitResults.messageBody:
The chatbot could only be used from a terminal. It now opens a window with
the conversation above and a text box below, so it can be used without one.

The chatbot's own logic is unchanged. What was missing was a way to get a
reply back as a string, since a window has to be handed the text to put in a
bubble whereas the console can just print it. Ui therefore gained a second
mode: Ui.forGui() collects replies instead of printing them, and
takeShownText() hands over everything shown since the last call. MattChatBot
exposes that through getResponse(), which handles one command and returns the
reply, reporting a failed command in the returned text rather than throwing
so that one bad command does not end the conversation.

On the GUI side, MainWindow is the controller, DialogBox is one message, and
both load their own FXML from src/main/resources/view. The bot's avatar sits
on the left and the user's on the right; the styling lives in main.css rather
than in the layout files.

Two details worth recording:

- Launcher exists so the program's main class is not itself an Application
  subclass. Without it the packaged JAR fails to start, complaining that the
  JavaFX runtime components are missing. This is the mistake the increment
  warns about.
- The JavaFX dependency list in the tutorial predates Apple Silicon. The
  mac-aarch64 classifier is needed alongside mac, or the app does not start
  on an M-series Mac.

Verified by rendering the window and driving it through adding, listing,
marking, finding, both error cases and bye, and by running the packaged JAR.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-Level-10'
Take varargs in TaskList.add
commitResults.messageBody:
Adding several tasks meant one call each, which is how a list gets set up
both in the tests and anywhere a batch is added at once. TaskList.add now
takes varargs and delegates to Collections.addAll, so those become one call.

A caller with a single task writes exactly what it wrote before, so nothing
else needed changing. The three-task fixture in TaskListTest is now one call,
and two tests cover the new cases: several tasks arriving in order, and the
empty call leaving the list alone.

Varargs was already used elsewhere for the same reason: Ui.show takes the
lines of a reply that way, and StorageTest.writeLines takes the lines of a
save file.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-Varargs'
